newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Indonesian minister shrugs off US delay on F-16s.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian minister shrugs off US delay on F-16s.

text.p: Indonesia's foreign minister Ali Alatas said on Tuesday that purchasing F-16s from the United States was not his country's top priority since it had never asked for the fighter jets in the first place.
The Clinton administration postponed the sale of at least nine F-16s to Indonesia until January because of Congressional objections to Jakarta's recent crackdown on political dissent.

Alatas, speaking to reporters at a luncheon, indicated U.S. President Bill Clinton was playing salesman for the F-16s during a Washington visit a year ago by President Suharto, which the foreign minister also attended.
Clinton, he said, asked the Indonesian leader if he wanted to buy some F-16s, which had been destined for Pakistan but not delivered.

Suharto told Clinton that "It's not our priority, we are one of the last ASEAN countries buying this kind of thing," Alatas said in reference to the 21-country Association of Southest Asian Nations. Even the tiny state of Singapore has a larger air force and navy than Indonesia, he added.
Subsequently he said U.S. officials offered "some very good terms so we started to say, "Okay what's the price."

"So when suddenly one or two senators made a big issue out of it and linked it to the latest developments in Indonesia -- which are highly exaggerated -- our natural reaction was: 'No problem, you don't want to sell them, we never asked for them in the first place,'" he said.
But, Alatas said that if the United States still wanted to sell the F-16s, Indonesia was still interested.
Alatas said earlier in Indonesia the original U.S. offer was for 24 fighters but Jakarta wanted only nine to add to the nine F-16s purchased previously.
In July, shortly after the Clinton administration agreed to sell the F-16s, Indonesia's military raided offices of opposition parties and arrested political activitists.

The raids sparked the worst riots in Jakarta in more than two decades and left at least five dead. Since then activists arrested in the riots were charges with subversion, which carries the death penalty.
Although it was unlikely Congress could have mustered enough votes to block the sale, the opposition of several prominent members caused the administration to put off the sale.
